items.title: What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores
items.summary:
Welcome back to our weekly behind-the-scenes glimpse at what’s getting our team talking. Tell us what you’ve been reading at info@reasonstobecheerful.world and we just might feature it here. 

Get smart 
 Over the last decade, the rise of smartphones across the U.S. has coincided with a significant drop in kids’ performance at school. Now, as the New York Times reports in a story shared by Executive Editor Will Doig, a new study has found that school phone bans are leading to modest improvements. Published this week by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard, the study included 3.3 million students in third through tenth grade, comparing the math and reading test scores of students at schools with and without strict phone bans.  

Though the gains seen at the schools with phone bans were modest, they suggest that gradual improvement is underway. 

Will says: 
 As a parent, there are so many reasons I’m in favor of banning phones at school, academics being just one of them. Still, it’s great to see data showing proof of concept on that aspect. 

Mapping roots 

In other phone-related news, there’s now an app that can help you find remarkable old trees. According to a Guardian article shared by Editorial Director Rebecca Worby, Ancient Trees offers a curated map of notable trees. 

“I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing,” the app’s creator, Hidde Burgmans, told the Guardian, “but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.” 

Becca says: 
 On the one hand, using an app takes away the serendipity of just happening into a notable…
items.t: What We’re Reading: Phone Bans Are Improving Kids’ Test Scores

items.title: ‘Everybody Wants to Rule the World’ sounds nothing like the Don Henley song that inspired it
items.summary:
Some decades are just bigger than others, but the 1980s might have outdone them all,  especially when it comes to music . From the ascendance of hip hop to the dominance of hair metal,  the era is filled with pop perfection . The early half of the decade was defined by the  massive “New Wave” invasion . Brilliant British bands crossed the Atlantic with clever synthesizers, angular rhythms, and stylish haircuts. Groups like Duran Duran, Depeche Mode, and  the Eurythmics totally reshaped the music charts .

Among these electronic pioneers stood Tears for Fears. Formed in England by Kent natives Roland Orzabal and Curt Smith, the duo released their critically acclaimed debut album,  The Hurting , in 1983. They established themselves as masters of moody, introspective synth-pop, climbing to the Top 5 of the U.K. charts with three singles from the album,  including the enduring “Mad World.”  

When it came time to record their second album, 1985’s  Songs from the Big Chair , the pressure on the pair of musicians was immense. Every single track took an agonizingly long time to put together. The band labored over every drumbeat, chord progression, and lyric. Some took an entire year to produce. 

Just as finishing up the record finally seemed within reach, their record label stepped in with a directive: add a catchy new track to boost crossover appeal in the United States. The surprising spark for what would become one of their most enduring hits came from an unlikely musical source: former Eagles drummer Don Henley.

The Don Henley groove that changed everything 

Scouring…
items.t: ‘Everybody Wants to Rule the World’ sounds nothing like the Don Henley song that inspired it

items.title: The Raiders’ rookie quarterback scored his first NFL touchdown. Thousands of fans stayed seated to honor his mom.
items.summary:
An unexpectedly sweet gesture from thousands of Las Vegas Raiders fans has brought football lovers around the country together, even from rival teams.

Rookie Raiders quarterback Fernando Mendoza landed his first NFL touchdown in a match-up against the Seattle Seahawks on November 15, 2026. But instead of leaping from their stadium seats to cheer, Raiders fans stayed seated to celebrate the big moment. Why? Because that’s what Mendoza’s parents do for every one of their son’s achievements.

View this post on Instagram 

Mendoza’s mom has multiple sclerosis and uses a wheelchair 

As a standout college quarterback in 2025, Mendoza became the first Heisman Trophy winner (an annual award recognizing the best college football player in the nation) from Indiana University. He was also the top NFL draft pick for the 2026 season. 

And in the background of all of those wins sat his mom, Elsa, who lives with multiple sclerosis, and his dad, Fernando Sr., who always sits in solidarity with her. 

Elsa Mendoza was diagnosed with MS in 2008 , when Fernando was just a young child. The disease has since progressed to the point where she uses a wheelchair for mobility. Fernando Sr. chooses to sit with his wife while others rise and cheer at games, keenly aware of how much it limits her view when everyone around her is standing.

Members of Raiders Nation take note and rally others to stay seated 

Many fans who entered Allegiant Stadium in Las Vegas for the game against the Seahawks were greeted by a man holding a sign asking people to stay seated during Mendoza’s first touchdown,…
items.t: The Raiders’ rookie quarterback scored his first NFL touchdown. Thousands of fans stayed seated to honor his mom.

items.title: Scientists spent 13 years watching jaguars. What they saw challenged a long-held belief.
items.summary:
Cats have a way of messing with our expectations. Even the humble house cat is proving itself to be less aloof and antisocial than we formerly thought. And it seems their much bigger relatives have a few surprises of their own.

Jaguars, for instance, have long been considered solitary animals, with males and females generally keeping their distance except during mating season and when mothers raise their cubs. But after watching jaguars for 13 years, researchers found evidence that these famously independent cats may have a more complicated social life than we realized.

The researchers conducted their work in Brazil’s Pantanal, a vast tropical wetland that supports one of the world’s highest jaguar densities. This provided a rare opportunity to observe individual cats repeatedly and see how their relationships developed over time.

Welcome to the Jaguar ‘coalition’ 

Jaguar resting on a tree. Photo credit: Canva 

The study found that, on occasion, male jaguars formed long-lasting partnerships, patrolling, eating, and resting together. Two of the recorded “coalitions,” as the researchers called them, lasted for more than seven years (beating out many Hollywood marriages).

These coalitions are still rare, and the data don’t suggest that jaguars are as close-knit as lions or cheetahs. But it does suggest that jaguar relationships are more intertwined than scientists once believed.

The 69 jaguars in the study existed in 13 distinct but connected clusters. Most interacted with only a few others, while certain individuals played key roles in keeping those groups connected.…
items.t: Scientists spent 13 years watching jaguars. What they saw challenged a long-held belief.

items.title: A first grader drew a butterfly. Then his classmates helped him see what he’d missed in the wings.
items.summary:
Parents and educators often walk a difficult line when it comes to getting the best out of kids. Push too hard or coach too harshly, and they might shut down. But going too easy does them just as much of a disservice.

However, when done right, teaching can make a world of difference. Not just in a long-term, intangible sort of way, either. The impact of steady, consistent feedback from teachers , parents, and even peers, when delivered the right way, can be downright jaw-dropping.

Famous teaching case study begins with drawing of a butterfly 

Educator Ron Berger was a longtime public school teacher before becoming the Director of EL Education, a K-12 nonprofit that advocates for school and curriculum reform.

Over his 25 years as an educator, there’s one lesson he carries with him that he continues to share with nearly everyone he meets.

The story is about Austin, a former student of Berger’s. Austin, a 1st grader at the time, was asked to draw a Western Tiger Swallowtail butterfly.

The Western tiger swallowtail butterfly. Photo credit: Wikimedia Commons 

His first attempt looked like any child’s drawing of a butterfly you’ve ever seen: big, round wings, beady little eyes, and no specific design or features to indicate the butterfly’s species.

But instead of giving Austin a gold star for effort and a pat on the back, Berger kept pushing his student. Or, more specifically, he asked Austin’s peers to push him.

Austin’s peers were asked for help through kind, specific feedback 

Berger asked Austin’s peers to help him improve his drawing through suggestions and…
items.t: A first grader drew a butterfly. Then his classmates helped him see what he’d missed in the wings.

An Instagram video posted by NBC LA News begins with a blonde woman making a bold statement: “I don’t want to say that the universe shut down aviation just so Michelle and I could become friends,” she declares. A chyron over the clip reads, “A friendship takes flight after the FAA ground stop.”

The clip bounces back to Chambers, who shares how odd things had begun to get at the airport. “And it even said ‘flight left’ on the screen, and I’m like, ‘No, it didn’t! We’re still here.’” She laughs and rolls her eyes. “So it seemed really eerie.”

items.title: A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire.
items.summary:
In the early hours of April 30, 1994, Joe Campbell walked to the phone booth near his home in Forest Gate, East London , to call his parents in Guyana. At first, he thought there was a discarded bag of chips inside.

It was a newborn girl, about two hours old, with her umbilical cord still attached. Campbell called 999 (the British version of 911) and stayed with her until help arrived.

He asked if he could adopt her, but he was told no, in part because he wasn’t married. But he gave her the name “April,” and for years he sent her birthday cards and presents until social services eventually asked him to stop. She was adopted by another family when she was 3.

She grew up knowing almost nothing about the man who found her until 2016, at age 22, she made a public appeal in the London newspaper Metro to find him.

A colleague at the delivery company where Campbell worked saw it and showed him.

View this post on Instagram 

“I ran home and [told] my daughter Rihanna on the phone, ‘I think I found April,’” Campbell recalled on Good Morning Britain .

They reunited that summer, and they’ve been family ever since. She changed her name to April, and she calls him Dad.

View this post on Instagram 

“Joe is complete family,” she said, according to SWNS . “His kids are my siblings now. We’re so close, we stay at each other’s houses. He never stopped thinking about me. I don’t know what this man is. An angel.”

Campbell is now 62 and still drives a bus. So April, a bank employee in West London, has started a fundraiser to help him retire early. The pair went back on Good Morning…
items.t: A man found a 2-hour-old baby in a London phone box in 1994. Now she’s raising money so he can retire.

items.title: British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time
items.summary:
On their JOLLY YouTube channel, content creators Josh and Ollie do all kinds of fun culture-clash experiments featuring food . They recently decided to see what British grandparents, or “coffin dodgers,” as they described themselves, would make of some classic Midwestern comfort food.

Midwestern cuisine tends to favor hearty, filling food with plenty of casseroles (also known as hotdishes), creamy sauces, and generous helpings of meat, cheese, and potatoes. Much of the region’s food traditions were shaped by European immigrants, particularly Germans and Scandinavians, as well as the ingredients and practical cooking styles that became common across the Midwest.

That might sound pretty familiar to a British palate. British cuisine has its own long history of hearty meals built around meat, potatoes, vegetables, gravy, and other comforting staples. But familiar ingredients don’t always make for familiar dishes. These grandparents’ reactions prove just how much room there is for cultural confusion at the dinner table.

First up were the appetizers, which included ranch dressing with vegetables, cheese curds, and “Minnesota sushi”  

Thanks to the World Cup , many non-Americans were introduced to ranch and became instantly obsessed, with some even trying to smuggle or ship it back home. This time around, the condiment was equally well received. The grandparents described it as “ubiquitous” and “cheeky but not flippant,” which is both hilarious and, somehow, a pretty good description of ranch.

“Minnesota sushi,” on the other hand, required a little more explanation. Despite…
items.t: British grandparents taste ‘Minnesota sushi,’ ‘puppy chow,’ and other Midwestern classics for the first time

items.title: A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health
items.summary:
It’s no secret that smartphones, YouTube, and iPads have dramatically changed what childhood looks like for Gen Z and Gen Alpha. Since smartphones and iPads came on the scene, kids have spent far less time outdoors. In 2009, 7% of children ages 6 to 17 spent an hour or less in nature. In 2025, that number has more than quadrupled to 26%.

A new study from the University of Exeter shows why it’s so important for kids to spend plenty of time outside, especially when they’re playing with others. Researchers found that children who grew up in the ‘90s and visited a park at least once a week scored 16.5% better on mental health assessments than those who did not.

Kids running on the playground. Photo credit: Canva 

The study used data from the Children of the 90s long-term cohort study. The study recruited more than 14,000 pregnant women from April 1991 to December 1992 and followed their children extensively for decades. 

Taking children to parks is great for their mental health 

“Our research suggests encouraging children to visit parks and playgrounds at least once a week could be a practical way to support their emotional wellbeing, social skills and mental health. But for this to work fairly, communities need good-quality parks that are safe, accessible and welcoming to families from all backgrounds,” lead researcher Mark Ferguson of the University of Exeter said in a statement .

“Parks give children space to be physically active, which is known to support mental and physical health, as well as helping adventurous and imaginative play to build confidence and…
items.t: A study of ’90s kids found that regular trips to the park are linked to 17 percent better mental health

items.title: Thieves stole 14-year-old’s lawn care business equipment. Kind strangers donated $37,000 to help.
items.summary:
Sonny Gallardo, 14, and his family stepped outside their Prairie Village, Kansas, home on Halloween to a shocking discovery: his precious (and pricey) lawn care equipment had been stolen overnight.

“I woke up, and my grandma said our equipment got stolen. I walked outside, and it was [gone],” Gallardo tells Upworthy. “I didn’t believe it at first. I still don’t. We assumed it was safe.”

The ninth-grader and his family, who founded his lawn-mowing and lawn-care business named Sunnyside Jobs, LLC, went to the police station to file a report. What happened next has left them shocked, humbled, and grateful.

View this post on Instagram 

Gallardo’s lawn care business beginnings 

Gallardo started mowing lawns when he was just 10 years old.

“I know how it feels to walk outside to a nice lawn,” he tells Upworthy. “It brings other people joy.”

With the help of his grandma Monica, his grandpa, two friends, and his aunt (who handles administrative work), the business expanded to offer power washing, leaf and junk removal, and more.

“We do everything,” Gallardo adds. “It’s fun. I just really like doing it. It’s satisfying to me, and [we mow] about 30-35 lawns.”

So when his equipment—including a 10-foot trailer with five lawn mowers on it, totaling over $20,000—was stolen, he was devastated. Until his community and kind strangers rallied around him.

Donations flood in for Gallardo 

Gallardo’s grandmother started a GoFundMe to help cover the costs of the arduous process of buying back his lawn-care equipment.

“They also cleared out everything from the back of the work…
items.t: Thieves stole 14-year-old’s lawn care business equipment. Kind strangers donated $37,000 to help.

items.title: A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home.
items.summary:
In 2019, a family in Los Angeles was getting ready to move to San Diego when their cocker spaniel, Corduroy, went missing .

“His disappearance broke their hearts, especially his best friend, Samantha’s young daughter,” Los Angeles Animal Services wrote in a social media post.

They moved without him, and seven years passed.

Then, in October, an older cocker spaniel came into LA Animal Services’ North Central Shelter . Nobody knows where Corduroy had been for all that time, but his microchip still led straight to his family, who were still living in San Diego.

They drove up to get him. “They made the trip from San Diego to bring him home, and the reunion was filled with hugs, smiles, and happy tears,” the shelter wrote, according to KTLA .

LA Animal Services shared two photos side by side: Samantha’s daughter as a little girl, hugging Corduroy on the steps, and the two of them together again seven years later.

“Corduroy’s story is a powerful reminder: microchips help bring lost pets home, even years later!” the shelter added.

It’s important to note that the chip only worked because the family’s contact information on it was still current. A microchip is just an ID number; if the phone number registered to it is no longer active, the scan leads nowhere. All six LA Animal Services shelters offer microchipping.

View this post on Instagram 

The post A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home. appeared first on Upworthy .
items.t: A Cocker Spaniel bolted during a move in 2019. Seven years later, a microchip brought him home.

items.title: The People Who Became Wildlife
items.summary:
W hat might it be like to be a bird? 

Initially Helen Lawy thought being a kestrel would mean freedom. “I love birds, and particularly kestrels — when they’re hovering, they have an amazing overview of the landscape,” she says. The kestrel’s extraordinarily flexible neck and head give it a sweeping view of the landscape, while its eyes can see ultraviolet light, which helps it detect the urine trails left by voles.  

“Immediately you’ve got a very different perspective,” Lawy says animatedly. 

Credit: Wayne Tuckwell / Shutterstock 
 A retired resident of Taunton, Lawy helps manage the 65-acre Longrun Meadow floodplain beside the River Tone in Somerset County, United Kingdom. When scientists asked for volunteers who wanted to attempt to view the landscape through an animal’s perspective, Lawy signed up and chose the reddish-brown kestrel, a small falcon. 

First she learned about the bird’s capabilities and habits. Then, over a period of several weeks, Lawy would spend hours sitting at the river’s edge and following the instructions of the “Animal Collaboration” guidebook she’d received: Sit still, pay attention, choose one sense that particularly matters to the animal. Because of the kestrels’ keen eyesight, Lawy would start with focusing on visual clues, then listen intently. “You become sort of hypervigilant,” she says. The guide asks people to not immediately categorize or explain what they are experiencing, but to simply notice. 

Once Lawy began trying to inhabit the bird’s perspective, the romantic notion of freedom disappeared. The bird needs shelter, rough…
items.t: The People Who Became Wildlife

items.title: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
items.summary:
I t is a Tuesday morning at Against Da Grain, a barbershop on a quiet street on Staten Island’s North Shore. Owner Sean White is rounding off a cut for a middle-aged Black man while another customer waits nearby. Around them, hairstylists work through a stream of clients; conversations move between jokes, social issues and the ordinary problems — and pleasures — of life. 

“It’s always usually like a community conversation inside of a barbershop,” White says.  

The shop hosts back-to-school giveaways, free haircut events and Christmas toy distributions, and partners with local organizations to connect residents with resources. White describes the shop as “like a third party to the community.” 

Against Da Grain was one of 22 Staten Island barbershops that participated in a hypertension screening program. Credit: Tolu Olasoji 
 That intermediary role also creates an opening for health care: a way to reach Black men through a place and relationships already woven into their everyday lives.  

Dr. Joseph Ravenell is the principal investigator of the Community-to-Clinic Linkage Implementation Program , or CLIP, which brought hypertension screenings into barbershops as part of an American Heart Association study. He remembers going with his father to Mr. Mike’s shop every other Saturday, where the same men returned over months and years. That repetition, he says, builds “a level of trust, a level of camaraderie” that can be difficult to reproduce in health care. Men talked there about sports, politics and relationships, but also about health, and Ravenell was struck by how…
items.t: Can Barbershops Turn Trust Into Better Health for Black Men?
